transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-03
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood SE), Lina (Velocity Stack Eng Mgr), Omar (Vel Stack DevOps), Priya (CTO), Sam (SRE)

Summary:
Quickwalkthrough of the Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), authentication patterns (API keys, SSO, KMS integration), CI secret handling, and a short demo of the Console + Optimize suggestions. Discussed Dedicated vs Hosted, private deployment constraints. Agreed on sandbox access and a technical deep-dive for private deployment.

Topics Covered:
- SDK quickstart (py/ts) and local env vars
- CI secret strategies and recommended workflows
- Console walkthrough: model pinning, rollouts, traces
- Optimize: batching/quant profiles and cost trade-offs
- Security: SOC2, SAML/SSO, KMS, audit logs
- Next steps and pilot plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intro from our side, I'm Jordan Lee, account exec; Maya and Evan from our solutions team. How's everyone?
[00:10] Lina: Hi, thanks. I'm Lina, engineering manager for the integrati— integration team here. Omar and Sam are ops, Priya is on for high-level.
[00:18] Priya: Hi all.
[00:20] Jordan: Awesome. Today we want to walk through the SDKs, auth and CI best practices, show the console, and then Optimize recommendations that can reduce token costs. We'll keep it practical.
[00:30] Maya: Quick note, we'll demo both Python and TypeScript snippets and share a repo. There may be a couple of audio flubs, our transcript might show K V cash instead of KV cache.
[00:40] Omar: Haha, that's fine. We're most concerned about the CI flow and private network options.
[00:45] Evan: Cool. Who's on the list of stakeholders who would need access?
[00:50] Lina: Eng, prod, security. Priya will want docs for SOC2 and data residency.
[00:55] Jordan: Noted. We'll attach those.

[01:05] Maya: Alright, quickjump to code. Python example: 'pip install redwood' (note: package name for the demo). Then set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var. Sample snippet: client = Redwood(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate("Summarize this PR") — streamed output, very similar to other SDKs.
[01:35] Sam: Is streaming supported in both SDKs? We want server-sent events into our lambda function.
[01:40] Maya: Yes, streaming is supported. In TypeScript you'd use the stream API and pipe it through your SSE handler. We'll send a small snippet for Lambda. There's also a note about chunked transfer and connection timeouts.

[02:00] Lina: For secrets in CI, we have GitHub Actions and GitLab runners. Best practice?
[02:06] Evan: We recommend storing the API key in your secret manager (GH Actions secrets / Vault). Do not hardcode. In CI, call the Redwood CLI or set ephemeral tokens. We also support short-lived session tokens for Dedicated.
[02:25] Omar: Short-lived tokens sound good. How do we rotate keys with minimal disruption?
[02:30] Maya: Two approaches: 1) Use our rotating token API via the control plane integrated with your KMS — calls our token endpoint to mint ephemeral creds. 2) For hosted quickstarts, swap keys with a canary deployment and pin the model variant in the console so you don't get a sudden runtime change.
[02:50] Omar: We run air-gapped in some customers, what about private on-prem?
[02:55] Evan: Private deployments are possible, yes. We offer a Private package that runs in your VPC or on-prem; it supports KMS/HSM integrations, RBAC and audit logs. For that we'd need a deeper session with your infra team to map network egress, certs, and storage.

[03:20] Lina: Can we see the console UI for model pinning and rollouts?
[03:25] Jordan: Yup, switching to the console now — I'm sharing the screen (note: link to the deck and sandbox repo: https://redwood.example/sandbox/velostack-sample).
[03:40] Jordan: Here you can create a route, select model variants, pin a particular model family and set canary rollout percent. You can also set fallback to a cheaper quantized variant if the primary fails.
[04:00] Priya: That's interesting — how does fallback impact latency?
[04:05] Maya: Fallback may increase latency slightly because the model variant might be on different capacity, but it keeps the app alive. Optimize will highlight latency vs cost trade-offs and recommend batching or quantization profiles based on historical sequence lengths.

[04:30] Lina: About caching — KV cache is crucial for us in chat-like workloads. How does Redwood handle prefix caching?
[04:36] Evan: We do automatic KV caching for session prefixes and reuse KV state across requests. The runtime exposes controls to set cache TTL and disable for sensitive prompts. Side note: sometimes the transcripting will show it as K V cash, sorry.
[04:50] Sam: Can cache be sharded in Dedicated? We've got multi-tenant scenarios on the same cluster.
[04:55] Maya: Yes, you can partition caches by customer id and enforce namespace isolation in Dedicated. We'll share the config YAML.

[05:15] Omar: From a network perspective, what egress do we need to allow for hosted mode?
[05:20] Evan: IP ranges for the region. We'll produce a CIDR list. For private we avoid egress but you'll still need NTP and CRL/OCSP for certs. We'll include a checklist.

[05:40] Lina: Data retention and logs — we need audit logs for compliance.
[05:45] Maya: Audit logs are available in the console and can be exported to your SIEM or S3/GCS. For Private, logs remain in your environment; for Hosted we retain per your contract and can forward to your logging endpoint. SOC2 docs will be attached.

[06:05] Priya: Encryption at rest? KMS?
[06:08] Evan: Yes, at-rest encryption using customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) is supported for Private and Dedicated. For hosted, we offer integration with major cloud KMS.

[06:20] Jordan: Quick demo of the SDK repo. We'll show CI snippet for GH Actions. Example: 
- name: Checkout
- name: Set REDWOOD_KEY (from secrets)
- run: pip install -r requirements.txt && python tests/smoke.py
We recommend not storing long-lived keys in the repo; use actions secrets or Vault and rotate.

[06:55] Omar: How does rate limiting interact with retries? We have bursty traffic.
[07:00] Maya: The client returns standard 429 codes and a recommended Retry-After. We have client-side retry helpers in the SDK with jittered backoff. For Dedicated customers we set higher quota limits and can tune based on throughput.

[07:20] Lina: Can you show Optimize suggestions?
[07:25] Jordan: Sure — Optimize analyzes token distributions and will suggest turning on 4-bit quantization for certain models, lower batch sizes for low-latency routes, or increasing batching for background bulk jobs. Here's an example from another customer: enabling prefix caching + 8k context model cut costs by ~38% with negligible regression on quality.
[07:50] Sam: Regression detection — how do we know if quantization degraded outputs?
[07:55] Maya: We tie evals to prompt suites. Optimize runs A/B evals and alerts on quality regressions; you can pin the golden model.

[08:10] Lina: Any known gotchas in the SDK for TypeScript?
[08:14] Evan: The main gotcha is stream handling in some older Node runtimes — we call it out in the README. Also ensure your bundler doesn't strip global fetch if you rely on it. We'll provide a polyfill snippet.

[08:30] Jordan: Alright, quick Q&A from the team?
[08:35] Priya: Will we be able to get PII redaction or masking built-in?
[08:40] Maya: We provide content filters and field-level redaction helpers in the pipeline; full PII redaction is often a bespoke step in the customer's pipeline. We can help design a pattern.

[08:55] Omar: What's the SLA for Dedicated?
[08:58] Jordan: Our Dedicated contracts include a 99.9% uptime SLA and latency SLOs based on instance sizes; we'll share the SLA appendix.

[09:10] Lina: For the sandbox, can we point to a small repo that runs both a Python fastapi example and a Node lambda?
[09:15] Jordan: Yes — the repo link in the notes (https://redwood.example/sandbox/velostack-sample) has a FastAPI app, a Node lambda example, GH Actions workflow, and cdktf/CFT examples. We'll grant access after this call.

[09:30] Evan: Also we'll drop a short-lived test key for you to avoid using prod creds. That key expires in 72 hours.

[09:40] Sam: If we move to private, what's the onboarding timeline?
[09:44] Maya: Typical private onboarding is 6–8 weeks: planning, infra prep, install window, smoke tests, and handoff. We can do accelerated timelines for API-only PoC in 1–2 weeks if you avoid custom KMS integration initially.

[10:00] Priya: Cost modeling — can we get a sample TCO comparing hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[10:05] Jordan: We'll produce a simple TCO model with assumptions on seq length, tokens per call, concurrency. I'll include that in the next email.

[10:20] Lina: Anything else around security posture?
[10:22] Evan: We'll include our pen test summary, SOC2 type II report, and the SSO/SAML configuration guide. For SAML we support IdP-initiated and SP-initiated flows; we also support SCIM provisioning.

[10:40] Jordan: Ok, recap & next steps: Jordan to share sandbox access, sample repo, SOC2 and SSO docs; Maya to schedule private-deploy deep dive with Omar; Velocity Stack to run a smoke test and surface perf numbers.
[11:00] Omar: Sounds good. I'll provision a VPC test subnet and confirm egress rules.
[11:05] Priya: We'll review the TCO.
[11:10] Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links and items.

[11:20] (end)

Notes about transcript: natural speech patterns present; occasional mis-attributions; some transcription errors around acronyms and product names intentionally left to mirror real meeting artifacts.
